messages.subject: custom stat question
parts:
Hi,

I have a dataset that has many observations within each country within
each age group. I would like to take the mean within country and
within age group and then have ggplot2 treat that as the dataset. I
thought that stat_summary could solve this, but I could not get it to
work. Here is a manual way to do it, but I would like to figure out
how to do it using a custom stat in ggplot2:

library(ggplot2)
mwe <- structure(list(index = c(10, 5, 9, 6, 9, 6, 4, 5, 8, 7, 10, 4,
10, 10, 10, 7, 7, 10, 8, 9, 8, 5, 8, 3, 10, 5, 3, 9, 10, 8, 3,
5, 8, 5, 8, 3, 7, 10, 6, 8), age = c(19L, 19L, 19L, 18L, 17L,
19L, 19L, 19L, 17L, 18L, 17L, 18L, 18L, 18L, 19L, 16L, 19L, 18L,
18L, 18L, 18L, 16L, 19L, 17L, 19L, 19L, 18L, 17L, 19L, 18L, 19L,
19L, 19L, 19L, 17L, 19L, 18L, 19L, 15L, 19L), country =
structure(c(29L,
63L, 27L, 27L, 23L, 34L, 4L, 13L, 56L, 24L, 62L, 52L, 38L, 15L,
13L, 53L, 5L, 38L, 53L, 39L, 38L, 5L, 63L, 4L, 42L, 45L, 42L,
56L, 3L, 36L, 51L, 56L, 10L, 4L, 56L, 35L, 39L, 38L, 29L, 34L
), .Label = c("Albania", "Algeria", "Argentina", "Armenia",
"Australia",
"Azerbaijan", "Bangladesh", "Belarus", "Bosnia and Herzegovina",
"Brazil", "Bulgaria", "Canada", "Chile", "China", "Colombia",
"Croatia", "Czech Republic", "Dominican Republic", "Egypt", "El
Salvador",
"Estonia", "Finland", "Georgia", "Germany", "Great Britain",
"Hungary", "India", "Indonesia", "Iran", "Iraq", "Israel", "Japan",
"Jordan", "Kyrgyzstan", "Latvia", "Lithuania", "Macedonia", "Mexico",
"Moldova", "Morocco", "New Zealand", "Nigeria", "Norway", "Pakistan",
"Peru", "Philippines", "Poland", "Puerto Rico", "Romania", "Russian
Federation",
"Saudi Arabia", "Serbia and Montenegro", "Singapore", "Slovakia",
"Slovenia", "South Africa", "South Korea", "Spain", "Sweden",
"Switzerland", "Taiwan", "Tanzania", "Turkey", "Uganda", "Ukraine",
"United States", "Uruguay", "Venezuela", "Vietnam", "Zimbabwe"
), class = "factor")), .Names = c("index", "age", "country"),
row.names = c("127673",
"161926", "19958", "19632", "64264", "135838", "43617", "49375",
"153287", "108969", "167803", "110840", "136636", "52138", "49599",
"151038", "1575", "74303", "150628", "76663", "75005", "1757",
"161296", "44008", "141830", "146433", "78691", "155310", "38752",
"72619", "148964", "155350", "45559", "44219", "153673", "71390",
"75843", "137775", "128038", "136409"), class = "data.frame")

mwe2 <-
with(mwe,aggregate(index,list(age=age,country=country),FUN="mean"))
mwe2$mean_index <- mwe2$x #x was produced by aggregate
(theplot <- ggplot(mwe2,aes(y=mean_index,x=age)) + geom_point() +
geom_smooth())


Thank you for any ideas!

Xu

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: custom stat question
parts:
Hi:

The introductory sentence of section 5.9 of Hadley's ggplot2 book
says: "It's often useful to be able to summarise the y values for each
unique x value. In ggplot2, this role is played by stat_summary()..."

In other words, ggplot2 can handle summaries of a response variable
wrt one (categorical) variable. In your code, the aggregate()
statement generated the mean of the level combinations of two
variables. AFAIK, the ability to summarize over more than one (factor)
variable isn't built into stat_summary().

One can do some very nice things with stat_summary(), but it was not
intended to make ggplot() or qplot() a 'one-stop shop' for general
data summarization and graphics. In your case, the way you did it is
best. The problem is that you're trying to average index by country at
a fixed age, but country isn't represented in the plot, so it would be
difficult for stat_summary() to produce the average. (I won't say
impossible, since someone could come along and say 'not so!', but it
would not be trivial). OTOH, this is a fairly trivial calculation in
ddply(), aggregate() or a half-dozen or so other summary functions
available in R. The other advantage of producing summaries prior to
plotting is that you can check them to see if they make sense.

It's often recommended to do the statistical summaries outside of
ggplot() since the function allows different data frames to be read in
different layers. In this case, you only need the summary data as
input to ggplot(), but in other cases it makes sense to pass the
entire data frame into ggplot() for certain layers of the plot and use
a summary data frame to produce additional layers of interest.

HTH,
Dennis

Dear Dennis,

Your reply helped a lot. Thank you very much for explaining
everything. I really appreciate your time.

I would still be interested in a purely ggplot2 way of doing this,
whether it be creating a new stat or something else.

Are there any resources that explain how to create custom stats?
Hadley's book does not go into much detail on this topic and I have
not found anything on the web.

Thanks!

Xu
